passage: Three days after matching with Chidi on a dating app in Manchester, Nour typed the message she had practised with her flatmate: "Before we chat more, can we do a quick video call? I do this with everyone." Earlier she had run his photos through an image search; they led only back to his own profile and a five-a-side football club page. Still, she waited for his reply with her thumb hovering over the block button. "Sure! Tonight at 8? Warning, my kitchen is a mess." At eight, there he was, real, laughing, a pan of jollof rice burning behind him. They talked for twenty minutes. Afterwards Nour texted her flatmate: "He's real, and he didn't mind at all." Her last match had sulked for days at the same question and then asked for help with "a customs fee". Nour had blocked that one. Her line stayed simple: no money and no private photos to anyone she had not met.

qa.q: Where did Nour's image search of Chidi's photos lead?
qa.a: Only back to his own profile and a five-a-side football club page.

qa.q: How was Nour feeling while waiting for Chidi's reply?
qa.a: Nour felt cautious and a little tense, thumb hovering over the block button in case he refused.

qa.q: Which of Nour's checks worked, and why?
qa.a: The image search and the early video call tested whether Chidi was real; his easy yes, unlike the last match's sulking and fee request, showed the difference.

qa.q: How might Chidi have seen the video-call request?
qa.a: Chidi seemed relaxed and even amused, joking about his messy kitchen, which suggests he saw it as a normal, fair check.

grounding: Shows a person asking for an early live video call and checking photos, and a genuine match accepting the checks without anger.

passage:
Monday, 2 a.m.
Sara says she's in a hospital in Istanbul after a car accident, her wallet stolen, and they won't treat her properly until someone pays. She cried on the voice note. Four months of good-night messages, and she never once asked me for anything, so it feels real.
I almost sent my whole scholarship. My finger was on the button.
Then I remembered Eshaan's face last week when I said she'd cancelled our video call again. He asked, gently, "Has she ever been on camera, even once?" She hasn't. Not once in four months.
I'm so scared she's really hurt and I'm abandoning her. I'm also scared I'm the fool in a story everyone has heard before. The worst part is I'd be too embarrassed to tell anyone either way.
I'm not sending anything tonight. I'm messaging Eshaan now, and in the morning I'll tell Abba too, even if it's awful.
Asif

qa.q: Where does Sara say she is?
qa.a: In a hospital in Istanbul after a car accident.

qa.q: What is Asif afraid of as the voice note sinks in?
qa.a: Asif is scared that Sara is really hurt and being abandoned, and also scared of being fooled, with embarrassment making it hard to tell anyone.

qa.q: What protective steps does Asif choose?
qa.a: Asif sends nothing tonight, messages Eshaan, and plans to tell Abba in the morning, pausing and bringing in trusted people before any money moves.

qa.q: How does Eshaan seem to see the relationship?
qa.a: Eshaan seems concerned but kind, gently asking whether Sara has ever been on camera, a quiet warning without mockery.

grounding: Shows a young adult in a warm long-distance bond who gets a sudden crisis story and a money request, torn by love, fear and shame.

subtype: Never send money to someone not met [Response]
passage: Selin was halfway through her shift at the bakery in Berlin when the message came: "Babe, my visa is stuck. I need gift cards today or I can't fly to you." For six weeks Daniel had been the best part of her evenings. Her stomach dropped, but her mind went to a line her sister often repeated: if someone you've never met asks for money, stop. She didn't reply. At break she showed Tuan, who worked the counter with her. He read it twice. "Gift cards for a visa? That's not how visas work." He didn't laugh or ask how she could fall for it. He just pulled up a chair. Together they took screenshots, reported the profile on the app, and filed an online report with the police. Selin felt sad and hollow, and a little foolish. Tuan bought her a pretzel. "You caught it before it cost you anything. That's the part that counts."

qa.q: What did Daniel say he needed the gift cards for?
qa.a: He said his visa was stuck and he couldn't fly to Selin without them.

qa.q: How did Selin feel after reporting it?
qa.a: Selin felt sad and hollow, and a little foolish, even though she had stopped in time.

qa.q: What made Selin's response a good one?
qa.a: She treated the money request as a stop sign, didn't reply, told a coworker, and reported the profile to the app and to the police.

qa.q: How did Tuan respond, and why does that matter?
qa.a: Tuan took it seriously without blame or mockery and helped report it, which makes it easier for Selin to seek help instead of hiding in shame.

grounding: Shows an adult treating a request for gift cards from an online partner as a stop sign, telling a friend and reporting it, and being supported rather than blamed.

subtype: Why the scammer builds a persona [Observer]
passage:
Shankar: hey, saw you in the bank queue again today. everything ok?
Jasleen: yeah, just sending something to Ethan. his parcel is stuck at customs
Shankar: the one posted overseas with the army? isn't this the third time?
Jasleen: fourth. but he'll pay it all back when he lands, he promised
Shankar: I'm not judging, I promise. can I ask a few things?
Jasleen: ok
Shankar: have you two ever video called? has anyone you know met him?
Jasleen: his camera's broken. and he's very private
Shankar: I read up on this after my cousin lost money. it's usually not one lonely guy. it's whole teams with scripts, fake photos, shifts. they're very good at it
Shankar: it's not about you being careless. they do this for a living
Jasleen: ...he did use the exact same line about his mother twice
Shankar: want to talk to the bank manager together tomorrow, before you send anything else? I'll come

qa.q: How many times has Jasleen sent money to Ethan?
qa.a: Four times.

qa.q: What seems to be driving Shankar's careful questions?
qa.a: Shankar seems worried but careful not to shame Jasleen, promising not to judge and explaining that the people behind this do it for a living.

qa.q: Why is asking questions better than scolding here?
qa.a: Questions let Jasleen notice the gaps, like the broken camera and the repeated line, without feeling blamed, and lead to a concrete step: the bank manager together.

qa.q: How might Jasleen feel as the doubts sink in?
qa.a: Jasleen may feel shaken and embarrassed on noticing the repeated line about Ethan's mother, but less alone because Shankar offers to come.

grounding: Shows a friend who notices repeated transfers to an unmet partner, asks gentle questions instead of scolding, and explains that such scams are organised work.

passage:
Friday
Sixty-two applications since March, and today someone finally wants me. "Data entry, work from home, two hours a day," the message said, with a salary bigger than Papa's. All I have to do is pay a registration fee by tonight and send my bank details "for salary setup".
I actually cried a bit. Relief, I think. I'm so tired of Mummy's face when relatives ask what I'm doing now.
Yash-bhaiya came in and I showed him. He didn't say it was fake straight away. He asked, "Which company? Did you apply to them?" I didn't. I'd never heard of them. The email is from some random free account. Two hours a day for that money... I wanted it to be true so badly I didn't let myself ask.
We looked up the company name together. Nothing. I'm not paying anything and not sending bank details. Tomorrow Yash-bhaiya and I will report the number, screenshots and all.
Payal

qa.q: How many applications had Payal sent since March?
qa.a: Sixty-two.

qa.q: Why did Payal almost believe the offer?
qa.a: Payal felt desperate and exhausted after so many applications, and the offer brought such relief that the questions got pushed aside.

qa.q: What checks helped, and what did Payal decide?
qa.a: Asking which company it was and whether Payal had applied, then searching the name, showed nothing real; Payal decided not to pay or share bank details and to report it.

qa.q: How did Yash-bhaiya help without making things worse?
qa.a: He didn't mock the offer; he asked simple questions and searched with Payal, so the discovery felt shared rather than shaming.

grounding: Shows a job seeker offered high pay for little work who is asked for a fee and bank details, with desperation making it easy to believe.

passage: Looking back, I should have said something in the first week. Yusuf, my lab partner, was glued to his phone between classes, liking videos and rating hotels for a "task group". Small amounts came into his account every day, and he'd show me, grinning. "Easy money, Maria. You should join." Then one evening in the canteen he went pale. The group said he had to deposit money to "unlock" his earnings, and he was about to borrow from his roommate. I remembered a notice the college had put up about exactly this pattern. I didn't want to sound like his mother, so I just showed him the notice and said, "I might be wrong, but this looks the same. Can we check before you pay?" He was quiet for a long minute. Then he left the group, and we went to the student welfare office to report it together. I'm glad I spoke, even that late.

qa.q: What did the group say Yusuf had to do to unlock his earnings?
qa.a: Deposit money.

qa.q: How did Maria feel about speaking up?
qa.a: Maria felt hesitant, not wanting to sound preachy, and later felt glad, while regretting not speaking in the first week.

qa.q: What made Maria's warning effective?
qa.a: Maria used the college notice, admitted possibly being wrong, and suggested checking before paying, so Yusuf could decide without feeling foolish.

qa.q: What might Yusuf have felt when he went pale in the canteen?
qa.a: Yusuf likely felt sudden fear and confusion, seeing his earnings locked just as he was about to borrow money.

grounding: Shows a student who sees a friend earning small payments for online tasks until a deposit is demanded, and warns kindly.

passage: In the kasba, Imran sat on the shop step with the offer letter on his phone: a supervisor job at a logistics company in Pune, joining after a "processing charge". The agent had also asked for a photo of his ID card, and whether his bank account could "receive company payments" for a few weeks. His sister Hafsa, who worked at the block office, read over his shoulder. "Real companies don't charge you to join," she said. Imran nodded; he had wondered the same. He opened the company's official website himself, not the link in the message, and called the number listed there. The HR person said they had no such vacancy and no agent in the district. Imran felt a flash of anger, then relief. He replied to the agent: "I don't pay for jobs, and nobody uses my account or my ID." Then he blocked the number and, with Hafsa, reported it on the government cyber-crime portal.

qa.q: What did the agent ask about Imran's bank account?
qa.a: Whether it could receive company payments for a few weeks.

qa.q: How did Imran feel after the call to HR?
qa.a: Imran felt a flash of anger at the trick, then relief at having checked before paying.

qa.q: Which step was the most protective, and why?
qa.a: Opening the official website himself and calling the listed number, rather than using the message link, let Imran verify the job independently.

qa.q: What might Hafsa have been thinking as she read the offer?
qa.a: Hafsa seemed alert and protective, sure that real companies don't charge to hire, and wanted Imran to check before trusting it.

grounding: Shows a person checking an employer through its official site, refusing to pay for a job, and refusing to let anyone use their bank account or ID.

passage:
Supervisor's note, accounts team, Monday.
For two weeks Zubin has been checking a group chat between tasks. Today he showed me screenshots: people posting "guaranteed profit every month" and photos of new bikes. He said he had put in a small amount first and got it back with profit within days, "so it's proven". He is now thinking of putting in his wedding savings before "the window closes Friday". He looked flushed and restless, and said everyone in the group is getting rich except him.
I didn't argue about numbers. I told him an early payout is often how these schemes win people over before bigger sums vanish, and asked whether the platform was registered with the regulator. He didn't know. I suggested he speak to an independent registered adviser, and to his family, before Friday, and I shared the regulator's public warning list.
He agreed to wait. I will check in with him on Wednesday.
Gurleen

qa.q: What happened with Zubin's first small amount?
qa.a: He got it back with profit within days.

qa.q: What was Zubin feeling as he talked about the group?
qa.a: Zubin seemed restless and anxious about missing out, flushed and convinced everyone was getting rich except him.

qa.q: What did Gurleen do that helped, without giving financial advice?
qa.a: Gurleen explained how early payouts build trust, asked about regulator registration, pointed Zubin to an independent registered adviser and his family, and planned a check-in.

qa.q: How might Zubin's family be affected if he rushed in before Friday?
qa.a: They could lose the wedding savings and face stress and shame, so including them before any decision protects them too.

grounding: Shows a person drawn in by screenshots of big gains, a small early payout and a deadline, feeling fear of missing out.

passage:
Sunday night
Ishita called again about her uncle's scheme: "Guaranteed returns, better than any bank, but only for people who join this week, and don't tell too many people." She's my closest friend from college, and she's so excited that I nearly said yes just not to disappoint her.
But three phrases kept bothering me: guaranteed, this week, don't tell. Anything real I've read about carries some risk, and nothing real needs to be kept quiet.
So instead of deciding, I looked up the scheme's name on the regulator's official website. Not registered. Then I called Mamaji, who has been a chartered accountant for years and has nothing to gain either way. He said, "Good that you paused. Don't let a deadline decide for you."
I texted Ishita: "I'm not joining, and I'm a little worried for you. Can we check it together?" She hasn't replied. That stings. But my stomach feels calm for the first time this week.
Santosh

qa.q: What did Santosh find on the regulator's official website?
qa.a: The scheme was not registered.

qa.q: What was Santosh feeling after texting Ishita?
qa.a: Santosh felt stung by Ishita's silence but calm inside for the first time that week.

qa.q: Which warning signs did Santosh notice, and what did Santosh do about them?
qa.a: Guaranteed, this week and don't tell; Santosh checked the regulator's website and asked Mamaji, an independent person with nothing to gain.

qa.q: How might Ishita feel reading Santosh's message?
qa.a: Ishita may feel hurt or defensive at first, since she was excited and it is her uncle's scheme, but the offer to check together leaves room to reconsider.

grounding: Shows an adult treating guaranteed returns, a rush and secrecy as warnings, checking regulator registration and consulting someone independent.

passage:
Counselling note, workplace wellbeing service, Thursday.
Saurabh came in looking exhausted; he said he hasn't slept properly in a week. Three weeks ago he moved most of his savings into an online trading scheme a colleague's friend recommended. The app showed rising profits until he tried to withdraw; now the account is "frozen" unless he pays a "release fee". He hasn't told his wife or parents. He said, "They'll think I'm an idiot," and that part of him wants to pay the fee to get it all back.
I said clearly that he was targeted by people who do this professionally, and that it says nothing about his intelligence. I explained that paying more usually leads to further loss, and that reporting early matters.
Today, with me, he filed a complaint on the national cyber-crime helpline and noted the regulator's complaint route. He agreed to tell his wife tonight, and asked if she could join our next session.
Pema

qa.q: What does the scheme say Saurabh must pay to unlock his account?
qa.a: A release fee.

qa.q: Why has Saurabh kept the loss from his family?
qa.a: Saurabh feels ashamed and afraid, worried that his wife and parents will think he's an idiot.

qa.q: What steps did Pema help Saurabh take?
qa.a: Pema said it said nothing about his intelligence, warned that paying more usually brings further loss, and helped him report to the cyber-crime helpline and note the regulator's route that day.

qa.q: How might Saurabh's wife feel when he tells her tonight?
qa.a: She may feel shocked, hurt and scared at first, but also relieved that he told her and that help is already under way.

grounding: Shows a person who lost savings to a fake scheme feeling shame and fear of the family's reaction and tempted to chase the loss, then reporting early and telling his wife.
